In [[mathematics]], '''topological recursion''' is a recursive definition of invariants of spectral curves.
It has applications in [[enumerative geometry]], [[random matrix theory]], [[mathematical physics]], [[string theory]], [[knot theory]].

== Introduction ==
The topological recursion is a construction in [[algebraic geometry]].<ref name=EO07>Invariants of algebraic curves and topological expansion, B. Eynard, N. Orantin, math-ph/0702045, ccsd-hal-00130963, Communications in Number Theory and Physics, Vol 1, Number 2, p347-452.</ref> It takes as initial data a [[spectral curve]]: the data of <math>\left(\Sigma,\Sigma_0,x,\omega_{0,1},\omega_{0,2}\right)</math>, where: <math>x:\Sigma\to\Sigma_0</math> is a covering of [[Riemann surface]]s with ramification points; <math>\omega_{0,1}</math> is a [[Meromorphic function|meromorphic]] [[Differential form|differential 1-form]] on <math>\Sigma</math>, regular at the [[Ramification (mathematics)|ramification points]]; <math>\omega_{0,2}</math> is a symmetric [[Meromorphic function|meromorphic]] bilinear [[Differential forms on a Riemann surface|differential form]] on <math>\Sigma^2</math> having a double pole on the diagonal and no residue.

The topological recursion is then a [[Recursive definition|recursive]] definition of infinite sequences of symmetric meromorphic n-forms <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> on <math>\Sigma^n</math>, with poles at ramification points only, for integers g≥0 such that 2g-2+n>0. The definition is a recursion on the integer 2g-2+n.

In many applications, the n-form <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> is interpreted as a [[generating function]] that measures a set of surfaces of [[Genus (mathematics)|genus]] g and with n boundaries. The recursion is on 2g-2+n the [[Euler characteristic]]s, whence the name "topological recursion".

[[File:Topological recursion illustration.png|Schematic illustration of the topological recursion: recursively adding pairs of pants to build a surface of genus g with n boundaries|thumb]]

== Origin ==
The topological recursion was first discovered in [[random matrix theory|random matrices]]. One main goal of random matrix theory, is to find the large size asymptotic expansion of n-point correlation functions, and in some suitable cases, the asymptotic expansion takes the form of a [[power series]]. The n-form  <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> is then the g<sup>th</sup> coefficient in the asymptotic expansion of the n-point correlation function. It was found<ref>B. Eynard, Topological expansion for the 1-hermitian matrix model correlation functions, JHEP/024A/0904, hep-th/0407261

A short overview of the ”Topological recursion”, math-ph/arXiv:1412.3286</ref><ref>A. Alexandrov, A. Mironov, A. Morozov, Solving Virasoro Constraints in Matrix Models, Fortsch.Phys.53:512-521,2005, arXiv:hep-th/0412205</ref><ref>L. Chekhov, B. Eynard, N. Orantin, Free energy topological expansion for the 2-matrix model, JHEP 0612 (2006) 053, math-ph/0603003</ref> that the coefficients <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> always obey the same recursion on 2g-2+n. The idea to consider this universal recursion relation beyond random matrix theory, and to promote it as a definition of [[Algebraic curve|algebraic curves]] invariants, occurred in Eynard-Orantin 2007<ref name=EO07 /> who studied the main properties of those invariants.

An important application of topological recursion was to [[Gromov–Witten invariants]]. Marino and BKMP<ref name=BKMP08>Vincent Bouchard, Albrecht Klemm, Marcos Marino, Sara Pasquetti, Remodeling the B-model, Commun.Math.Phys.287:117-178,2009</ref> conjectured that [[Gromov–Witten invariants]] of a toric [[Calabi–Yau manifold|Calabi–Yau]] 3-fold <math>\mathfrak X</math> are the TR invariants of a spectral curve that is the mirror of <math>\mathfrak X</math>.

Since then, topological recursion has generated a lot of activity in particular in [[enumerative geometry]].
The link to [[Givental formalism]] and [[Frobenius manifolds]] has been established.<ref>P. Dunin-Barkowski, N. Orantin, S. Shadrin, L. Spitz, "Identification of the Givental formula with the spectral curve topological recursion procedure", Commun.Math.Phys. 328 (2014) 669-700.</ref>

== Definition ==

(Case of simple branch points. For higher order branchpoints, see the section [[#Higher order ramifications|Higher order ramifications]] below)

*  For <math>n\geq 1</math> and <math>2g-2+n>0</math>:
<math display="block">\begin{align}\omega_{g,n}(z_1,z_2,\dots,z_{n}) &=\sum_{a=\text{branchpoints}} \operatorname{Res}_{z\to a} K(z_1,z,\sigma_a(z)) \Big( \omega_{g-1,n+1}(z,\sigma_a(z),z_2,\dots,z_n) \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad + \mathop{{\sum}'}_{\overset{g_1+g_2=g}{I_1\uplus I_2=\{z_2,\dots,z_n\} }} \omega_{g_1,1+\# I_1}(z,I_1)\omega_{g_2,1+\# I_2}(\sigma_a(z),I_2) \Big) \end{align}</math>
where <math>K(z_1,z_2,z_3)</math> is called the recursion kernel:
<math>
K(z_1,z_2,z_3) = \frac{\frac12 \int_{z'=z_3}^{z_2} \omega_{0,2}(z_1,z')}{\omega_{0,1}(z_2)-\omega_{0,1}(z_3)}
</math>
<br />
and <math>\sigma_a</math> is the local Galois involution near a branch point <math>a</math>, it is such that <math>x(\sigma_a(z))=x(z)</math>.
The primed sum <math>{\sum}'</math> means excluding the two terms <math>(g_1,I_1)=(0,\emptyset)</math> and <math>(g_2,I_2)=(0,\emptyset)</math>.

* For <math>n=0</math> and <math>2g-2>0</math>:
<br />
<math> F_g = \omega_{g,0} = \frac{1}{2-2g}\ \sum_{a=\text{branchpoints}} \operatorname{Res}_{z\to a} F_{0,1}(z) \omega_{g,1}(z)
</math>
<br />
with <math>dF_{0,1}=\omega_{0,1}</math> any antiderivative of <math>\omega_{0,1}</math>.

* The definition of <math>F_0=\omega_{0,0}</math> and <math>F_1=\omega_{1,0}</math> is more involved and can be found in the original article of Eynard-Orantin.<ref name=EO07 />

== Main properties ==

* '''Symmetry:''' each <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> is a symmetric <math>n</math>-form on <math>\Sigma^n</math>.
* '''poles:''' each <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> is meromorphic, it has poles only at branchpoints, with vanishing residues.
* '''Homogeneity:''' <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> is homogeneous of degree <math>2-2g-n</math>. Under the change <math>\omega_{0,1}\to \lambda \omega_{0,1}</math>, we have  <math>\omega_{g,n}\to \lambda^{2-2g-n}\omega_{g,n}</math>.
* '''Dilaton equation:'''
<math>\sum_{a=\text{branchpoints}} \operatorname{Res}_{z\to a} F_{0,1}(z)\ \omega_{g,n+1}(z_1,\dots,z_n,z)  = (2g-2+n) \omega_{g,n}(z_1,\dots,z_n) </math><br /> where <math>dF_{0,1}=\omega_{0,1}</math>.

* '''Loop equations:''' The following forms have no poles at branchpoints
<math>\sum_{z\in x^{-1}(x)} \omega_{g,n+1}(z,z_1,\dots,z_n) </math><br />
<math>\sum_{\{z\neq z'\} \subset x^{-1}(x)}
\Big(\omega_{g,n+1}(z,z',z_2,\dots,z_n)
+ \sum_{\overset{g_1+g_2=g}{I_1\uplus I_2=\{z_2,\dots,z_n\} }} \omega_{g_1,1+\# I_1}(z,I_1)\omega_{g_2,1+\# I_2}(z',I_2)
\Big)</math>
<br>
where the sum has no prime, i.e. no term excluded.

* '''Deformations:''' The <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> satisfy deformation equations
* '''Limits:''' given a family of spectral curves <math>\mathcal S_t</math>, whose limit as <math>t\to 0</math> is a singular curve, resolved by rescaling by a power of <math>t^\mu </math>, then <math>\lim_{t\to 0} t^{(2-2g-n)\mu}\omega_{g,n}(\mathcal S_t) =  \omega_{g,n}(\lim_{t\to 0} t^\mu \mathcal S_t) </math>.
* '''Symplectic invariance:''' In the case where <math>\Sigma</math> is a compact algebraic curve with a marking of a symplectic basis of cycles, <math>x</math> is meromorphic and <math>\omega_{0,1}=ydx</math> is meromorphic and  <math>\omega_{0,2}=B</math> is the fundamental second kind differential normalized on the marking, then the spectral curve <math>\mathcal S=(\Sigma,\mathbb C,x,ydx,B)</math> and <math>\tilde{\mathcal S}=(\Sigma,\mathbb C,y,-xdy,B)</math>, have the same <math>F_g</math> shifted by some terms.
* '''Modular properties:''' In the case where <math>\Sigma</math> is a compact algebraic curve with a marking of a symplectic basis of cycles,  and  <math>\omega_{0,2}=B</math> is the fundamental second kind differential normalized on the marking, then the invariants <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> are quasi-modular forms under the modular group of marking changes. The invariants <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> satisfy BCOV equations.{{clarify|date=March 2021 |reason=it is not clear what BCOV means}}

== Generalizations ==

=== Higher order ramifications ===

In case the  branchpoints are not simple, the definition is amended as follows<ref>V. Bouchard, B. Eynard, "Think globally, compute locally", JHEP02(2013)143.</ref> (simple branchpoints correspond to k=2):
<br />

<math>
\begin{align}
\omega_{g,n}(z_1,z_2,\dots,z_{n}) = 
&\sum_{a=\text{branchpoints}} \operatorname{Res}_{z\to a} 
\sum_{k=2}^{{\rm order}_x(a)} \sum_{J \subset x^{-1}(x(z))\setminus\{z\},\,\# J=k-1}
K_k(z_1,z,J) \\ 
& \qquad \cdot\sum_{J_1,\dots , J_\ell \vdash J\cup\{z\}} \sum'_{\overset{g_1+\dots+g_\ell=g+\ell-k}{I_1\uplus \dots I_\ell=\{z_2,\dots,z_n\} }} \prod_{i=1}^l \omega_{g_i,\# J_i+\# I_i}(J_i,I_i)
\end{align}
</math>

<br />
The first sum is over partitions <math>J_1,\dots,J_\ell</math> of <math>J\cup\{z\}</math> with non empty parts <math>J_i\neq \emptyset</math>, and in the second sum, the prime means excluding all terms such that <math>(g_i,\# J_i+\# I_i)=(0,1)</math>.

<math>K_k</math> is called the recursion kernel:
<br />
<math>
K_k(z_0,z_1,\dots,z_k) = \frac{\int_{z'=*}^{z_1} \omega_{0,2}(z_0,z')}{\prod_{i=2}^k (\omega_{0,1}(z_1)-\omega_{0,1}(z_i))}
</math>
<br />
The base point * of the integral in the numerator can be chosen arbitrarily in a vicinity of the branchpoint, the invariants <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> will not depend on it.

== Topological recursion invariants and intersection numbers ==

The invariants <math>\omega_{g,n}</math> can be written in terms of intersection numbers of [[Tautological ring|tautological]] classes:<ref name=Ey11>B. Eynard, Invariants of spectral curves and intersection theory of moduli spaces of complex curves, math-ph: arxiv.1110.2949, Journal Communications in Number Theory and Physics, Volume 8, Number 3.</ref>
<br />
(*) <math>
\begin{align}
\omega_{g,n}(z_1,\dots,z_n)
= 2^{3g-3+n} &\sum_{G=\text{Graphs}} \frac{1}{\#\text{Aut}(G)} \int_{\left(\prod_{v=\text{vertices}} {\overline{\mathcal M}}_{g_v,n_v} \right)}\,\, \prod_{v=\text{vertices}} e^{\sum_k \hat t_{\sigma(v),k} \kappa_k} \\ &\prod_{(p,p')=\text{nodal points}} \left(\sum_{d,d'} B_{\sigma(p),2d;\sigma(p'),2d'} \psi_p^d \psi_{p'}^{d'}\right) \prod_{p_i=\text{marked points}\, i=1,\dots,n} \left(\sum_{d_i} \psi_{p_i}^{d_i} d\xi_{\sigma(p_i),d_i}(z_i) \right)
\end{align}
</math><br />
where the sum is over dual graphs of [[Moduli of algebraic curves|stable nodal Riemann surfaces]] of total arithmetic genus <math>g</math>, and <math>n</math> smooth labeled marked points <math>p_1,\dots,p_n</math>, and equipped with a map <math>\sigma:\{\text{vertices}\}\to \{\text{branchpoints}\} </math>.
<math>\psi_p=c_1(\mathcal L_p)</math> is the [[Chern class]] of the [[Cotangent bundle|cotangent line bundle]] <math>\mathcal L_p</math> whose fiber is the cotangent plane at <math>p</math>.
<math>\kappa_k</math> is the <math>k</math><sup>th</sup> Mumford's kappa class.
The coefficients <math>\hat t_{a,k}</math>, <math>B_{a,k;a',k'}</math>, <math>d\xi_{a,k}(z)</math>, are the Taylor expansion coefficients of <math>\omega_{0,1}</math> and <math>\omega_{0,2}</math> in the vicinity of branchpoints as follows:
in the vicinity of a branchpoint <math>a</math> (assumed simple), a local coordinate is <math>\zeta_a(z)=\sqrt{x(z)-a}</math>. The Taylor expansion of <math>\omega_{0,2}(z,z')</math> near branchpoints <math>z\to a</math>, <math>z'\to a'</math> defines the coefficients <math>B_{a,d;a',d'}</math><br />
<math>\omega_{0,2}(z,z') \mathop{{\sim}}_{z\to a,\ z'\to a'} \left( \frac{\delta_{a,a'} }{(\zeta_a(z)-\zeta_{a'}(z'))^2}+ 2\pi \sum_{d,d'=0}^\infty \frac{B_{a,d;a',d'}}{\Gamma(\frac{d+1}{2})\Gamma(\frac{d'+1}{2})}\, \zeta_a(z)^d \zeta_{a'}(z')^{d'} \right) d\zeta_a(z)d\zeta_{a'}(z')</math>.
<br />
The Taylor expansion at <math>z'\to a</math>, defines the 1-forms coefficients <math>d\xi_{a,d}(z)</math><br />
<math>d\xi_{a,d}(z) =  \frac{-\Gamma(d+\frac12)}{\Gamma(\frac12)} \operatorname{Res}_{z'\to a} (x(z')-a)^{-d-\frac12}\omega_{0,2}(z,z')</math>
whose Taylor expansion near a branchpoint <math>a'</math> is <br />
<math> d\xi_{a,d}(z) \mathop{{\sim}}_{z\to a'}  \frac{-\delta_{a,a'} (2d+1)!! d\zeta_a(z)}{2^d \zeta_a(z)^{2d+2}}+ \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{B_{a,2d;a',2k} 2^{k+1}}{(2k-1)!!}\zeta_{a'}(z)^{2k} d\zeta_{a'}(z) </math>.
<br />
Write also the Taylor expansion of <math>\omega_{0,1}</math><br />
<math> \omega_{0,1}(z) \mathop{{\sim}}_{z\to a} \sum_{k=0}^\infty t_{a,k}\ \frac{\Gamma(\frac12)}{(k+1)\Gamma(\frac{k+1}{2})}\ \zeta_{a}(z)^{k} d\zeta_{a}(z) </math>.<br />
Equivalently, the coefficients <math>t_{a,k}</math> can be found from expansion coefficients of the [[Laplace transform]], and the coefficients <math>\hat t_{a,k}</math> are the expansion coefficients of the log of the Laplace transform<br />
<math>  \int_{x(z)-x(a)\in \mathbb R_+} \omega_{0,1}(z) e^{-u x(z)} = \frac{e^{-ux(a)}\sqrt\pi}{2 u^{3/2}} \sum_{k=0}^\infty t_{a,k} u^{-k}
= \frac{e^{-ux(a)}\sqrt\pi}{2 u^{3/2}} e^{-\sum_{k=0}^\infty \hat t_{a,k} u^{-k}}
</math> .

For example, we have<br />
<math>
\omega_{0,3}(z_1,z_2,z_3) = \sum_a e^{\hat t_{a,0}}   d\xi_{a,0}(z_1)d\xi_{a,0}(z_2)d\xi_{a,0}(z_3).
</math>

<math>
\omega_{1,1}(z) = 2 \sum_a e^{\hat t_{a,0}}  \left( \frac{1}{24} d\xi_{a,1}(z) + \frac{\hat t_{a,1}}{24} d\xi_{a,0}(z) +\frac12 B_{a,0;a,0} d\xi_{a,0}(z)\right).
</math>

The formula (*) generalizes [[ELSV formula|ELSV]] formula as well as [[David Mumford|Mumford]]'s formula and [[Marcos Marino|Mariño]]-[[Cumrun Vafa|Vafa]] formula.

== Some applications in enumerative geometry ==

=== Mirzakhani's recursion ===
[[Maryam Mirzakhani|M. Mirzakhani's]] recursion for hyperbolic volumes of [[Moduli space of algebraic curves|moduli spaces]] is an instance of topological recursion.
For the choice of spectral curve 
<math>\left(\mathbb C; \ \mathbb C;\ x: z\mapsto z^2 ;\ \omega_{0,1}(z)=\frac{4}{\pi} z \sin{(\pi z)} dz;\,\omega_{0,2}(z_1,z_2) = \frac{dz_1 dz_2}{(z_1-z_2)^2}\right) </math>
<br />
the n-form <math>\omega_{g,n} = d_1 \dots d_n F_{g,n}</math> is the Laplace transform of the [[Weil–Petersson metric|Weil-Petersson volume]]
<br />
<math>
F_{g,n}(z_1,\dots,z_n) = \int_0^\infty e^{-z_1L_1} dL_1  \dots \int_0^\infty e^{-z_nL_n} dL_n    \quad \int_{\mathcal M_{g,n}(L_1,\dots,L_n)} w
</math>
<br />
where <math>\mathcal M_{g,n}(L_1,\dots,L_n)</math> is the moduli space of hyperbolic surfaces of genus g with n geodesic boundaries of respective lengths <math>L_1,\dots,L_n</math>, and <math>w</math> is the Weil-Petersson [[volume form]].
<br />
The topological recursion for the n-forms <math>\omega_{g,n}(z_1,\dots,z_n)</math>, is then equivalent to Mirzakhani's recursion.

=== [[Witten conjecture|Witten–Kontsevich]] intersection numbers ===
For the choice of spectral curve 
<math>\left(\mathbb C; \ \mathbb C;\ x: z\mapsto z^2 ;\ \omega_{0,1}(z)=2z^2 dz;\,\omega_{0,2}(z_1,z_2) = \frac{dz_1 dz_2}{(z_1-z_2)^2}\right) </math>
<br />
the n-form <math>\omega_{g,n}= d_1 \dots d_n F_{g,n}</math> is
<br />
<math>
F_{g,n}(z_1,\dots,z_n) = 2^{2-2g-n}\sum_{d_1+\dots+d_n=3g-3+n} \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{(2d_i-1)!! }{z_i^{2d_i+1}} \quad \left\langle\tau_{d_1}\dots\tau_{d_n}\right\rangle_g
</math>
<br />
where <math>\left\langle\tau_{d_1}\dots\tau_{d_n}\right\rangle_g</math> is the [[Witten conjecture|Witten-Kontsevich]] intersection number of [[Chern class]]es of cotangent line bundles in the compactified [[Moduli of algebraic curves|moduli space of Riemann surfaces]] of genus g with n smooth marked points.

=== Hurwitz numbers ===
For the choice of spectral curve 
<math>\left(\mathbb C; \ \mathbb C;\ x:z \mapsto -z+\ln{z} ;\ \omega_{0,1}(z)=(1-z) dz;\,\omega_{0,2}(z_1,z_2) = \frac{dz_1 dz_2}{(z_1-z_2)^2}\right) </math>
<br />
the n-form <math>\omega_{g,n}= d_1 \dots d_n F_{g,n}</math> is
<br />
<math>
F_{g,n}(z_1,\dots,z_n) = \sum_{\ell(\mu)\leq n} m_\mu(e^{x(z_1)},\dots,e^{x(z_n)})  \quad h_{g,\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n}
</math>
<br />
where <math>h_{g,\mu}</math> is the connected simple [[Hurwitz number]] of genus g with ramification <math>\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n)</math>: the number of branch covers of the [[Riemann sphere]] by a genus g connected surface, with 2g-2+n simple ramification points, and one point with ramification profile given by the partition <math>\mu</math>.

=== Gromov–Witten numbers and the BKMP conjecture ===

Let <math>\mathfrak X</math> a toric [[Calabi–Yau manifold|Calabi–Yau]] 3-fold, with Kähler moduli <math>t_1,\dots,t_{b_2(\mathfrak X)}</math>.
Its [[mirror manifold]] is singular over a complex plane curve <math>\Sigma</math> given by a polynomial equation <math>P(e^x,e^y)=0</math>, whose coefficients are functions of the Kähler moduli.
For the choice of spectral curve 
<math>\left(\Sigma; \ \mathbb C^*;\ x ;\ \omega_{0,1}=y dx;\,\omega_{0,2} \right) </math> with <math>\omega_{0,2}</math> the fundamental second kind differential on <math>\Sigma</math>, 
<br />
According to the BKMP<ref name=BKMP08 /> conjecture, the n-form <math>\omega_{g,n}= d_1 \dots d_n F_{g,n}</math> is
<br />
<math>
F_{g,n}(z_1,\dots,z_n) = \sum_{\mathbf d\in H_2(\mathfrak X,\mathbb Z)} \sum_{\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n\in H_1(\mathcal L,\mathbb Z)} t^d \prod_{i=1}^n e^{x(z_i)} 
\mathcal N_{g}(\mathfrak X,\mathcal L;\mathbf d,\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n)
</math>
<br />
where 
<math>
\mathcal N_{g}(\mathfrak X,\mathcal L;\mathbf d,\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n)
= \int_{[{\overline{\mathcal M}}_{g,n}(\mathfrak X,\mathcal L, \mathbf d,\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n)]^{\rm vir}} 1
</math>
<br />
is the genus g Gromov–Witten number, representing the number of holomorphic maps of a surface of genus g into <math>\mathfrak X</math>, with n boundaries mapped to a special  Lagrangian submanifold <math>\mathcal L</math>. <math>\mathbf d=(d_1,\dots,d_{b_2(\mathfrak X)})</math> is the 2nd [[relative homology]] class of the surface's image, and <math>\mu_i\in H_1(\mathcal L,\mathbb Z)</math> are homology classes (winding number) of the boundary images.
<br />
The BKMP<ref name=BKMP08 /> conjecture has since then been proven.
